passage: The popular belief that memory works like a recording, faithfully storing experiences for later playback, has been steadily eroded by laboratory research. Psychologists studying recall have shown repeatedly that remembering is an act of reconstruction. Each time a memory is retrieved, it is subtly altered by the circumstances of the retrieval, by what the person has learned since the original event, and even by the questions they are asked. This does not make memory useless. Most of what we recall is broadly accurate, and the mechanism serves a practical purpose: it allows us to extract the meaning of events rather than to store every detail. The difficulty arises when confidence and accuracy come apart. Witnesses can feel entirely certain about details that were in fact suggested to them afterwards, and their certainty is often indistinguishable from the certainty of a correct recollection. For this reason, researchers caution that vividness should never be mistaken for reliability.
q: What does the writer say about the reconstructive nature of memory?
options: It allows us to extract meaning from events
explain: CAE · Reading P5 (opción múltiple): «it allows us to extract the meaning of events».

passage: The decision to build a second airport for the region has divided opinion more sharply than any infrastructure project in a generation. Its backers present it as an inevitable response to a population that has grown faster than the existing facilities can accommodate. Without new capacity, they argue, airlines will simply redirect routes elsewhere, costing the region jobs and investment that are hard to recover. An independent review, published last month, concluded that the forecasts were optimistic but not unreasonable, a verdict that each camp has since cited in support of its position.

That demand has levelled off and expansion would be cheaper
That the region has no need for air travel

passage: Few objects in the museum's collection provoke as much discussion as a small bronze figure of uncertain date, displayed near the entrance. Curators initially attributed it to a regional workshop of the early medieval period, a conclusion based largely on stylistic comparisons. Subsequent X-ray analysis, however, revealed that the figure had been cast over an earlier core, a technique rarely documented in that region. Some specialists now argue that the piece is a sophisticated later imitation, made to resemble an older work for a private collector. Others counter that the technique was more widespread than the surviving evidence suggests, and that absence of proof is not proof of absence. The museum has declined to revise the label, preferring to present both interpretations side by side, a decision that visitors appear to find more engaging than a definitive answer would be.
q: Why was the figure's date reconsidered?
options: X-ray analysis revealed an unusual casting technique
explain: CAE · Reading P5 (opción múltiple): La radiografía mostró una técnica de fundición poco documentada.

passage: The notion that language is a neutral vehicle for thought, merely clothing ideas that exist independently of it, has come under sustained challenge. Anthropologists working among communities with very different grammatical habits have observed that speakers attend to aspects of experience that others routinely ignore. Speakers of languages that require a precise indication of the source of information, for instance, tend to track evidentiality with a care that surprises outsiders. Yet the strongest version of the relativist claim, that language rigidly determines what can be thought, is difficult to sustain. Bilingual speakers can usually express the same idea in either tongue, albeit with differing emphasis, and translators routinely bridge conceptual gaps that were supposed to be insurmountable. The more defensible position, many now argue, is that language does not dictate thought so much as nudge habitual attention in particular directions, a subtle influence that is easy to overstate in either direction.
q: What is the 'strongest version' of the relativist claim?
options: That language is a neutral vehicle
That language rigidly determines what can be thought
explain: CPE · Reading P3 (opción múltiple): Afirma que la lengua determina rígidamente el pensamiento; el texto la considera difícil de sostener.

passage: Historians of the Industrial Revolution have traditionally emphasised the role of invention, picturing inventors as solitary geniuses whose machines transformed production overnight. Recent scholarship has complicated this picture considerably. Many of the crucial advances were incremental, the product of countless small adjustments by artisans who knew their materials intimately and who often had no formal training. Patents, moreover, were far less significant than is commonly assumed; many innovations were freely copied, and some of the most profitable ones were kept secret rather than protected. What distinguished Britain, on this view, was not a superior supply of geniuses but a dense web of workshops, informal networks and practical know-how that allowed good ideas to be tested, refined and disseminated quickly. The celebrated inventor, in other words, was often less the source of change than its most visible beneficiary.
q: According to recent scholarship, what distinguished Britain?
options: A dense web of workshops and practical know-how
explain: CPE · Reading P3 (opción múltiple): «a dense web of workshops, informal networks and practical know-how».

passage: Ethicists have long debated whether the obligation to help a stranger in distress is stronger when the one who could help is nearby and the cost is trivial. Empirical studies suggest that proximity matters far more than philosophers might like to admit: people are markedly more likely to intervene when the victim is visible and the bystander is alone, and considerably less so in crowds, where each individual assumes that someone else will act. Some have concluded that moral behaviour is largely situational, a product of circumstance rather than character. This inference, however, overlooks a crucial distinction. Situational pressures may determine whether a person acts in a given moment, while character shapes which pressures they notice and how they interpret them. Cost is the only factor that matters

q: Coloca el fragmento correcto en cada hueco. Sobran dos.
paras: Many people assume that learning a language is mainly about memorising vocabulary. In reality, progress depends far more on regular, everyday practice.
For instance, listening to podcasts on the way to work can improve your understanding without taking up any extra time.
Speaking with native speakers is also valuable, although many learners feel nervous at first.
Above all, it is important to accept that mistakes are part of the process and to learn from them.
With time, these small habits add up to a level of fluency that no course could provide on its own.

frags.A: Therefore, a little practice every day is far more effective than long sessions once a week.
frags.B: Writing a short diary entry each evening is another simple habit that builds fluency.
frags.C: Online conversation groups make this easier, because the atmosphere is usually relaxed.
frags.D: Vocabulary lists, by contrast, rarely help people use words in real situations.

q: Coloca el fragmento correcto en cada hueco. Sobra uno.
paras: Across the world, city residents are turning empty lots and rooftops into vegetable gardens. The movement is often presented as a purely environmental initiative, yet its effects reach much further.
Community gardens, for example, give neighbours a shared project that brings together people who might otherwise never speak to one another.
Critics, however, question whether such projects make a measurable difference to food supplies or carbon emissions in dense urban areas.
Supporters respond that the gains are social rather than statistical, and that a sense of belonging is itself worth protecting.
Whether or not the harvests are substantial, the gardens have changed how many residents think about the space they share.
Ultimately, the question is less about lettuce than about who gets to shape the city in which they live.

frags.A: Yet the appeal is not only about what is grown, but about who does the growing.
frags.B: Such initiatives also depend heavily on volunteers, which makes them vulnerable when enthusiasm fades.
frags.C: Planners, meanwhile, have begun to treat green spaces as infrastructure rather than decoration.
frags.D: Researchers have tried to measure these benefits, although the results remain difficult to interpret.
frags.E: In some cities, the authorities now provide land and water to encourage the practice.
frags.F: Many of the original gardeners, incidentally, had never grown anything before.

explain: El fragmento F sobra.

q: Coloca el fragmento correcto en cada hueco. Sobra uno.
paras: Few people stop to consider how much the English they speak today differs from the English of their great-grandparents. Yet the language has been changing constantly for over a thousand years.
Most of these changes go unnoticed because they arrive gradually, one generation at a time, and are rarely announced by anyone.
Purists have long lamented each new word or construction, treating them as signs of decline rather than as a natural process.
Linguists, by contrast, tend to regard such innovation as evidence of a living language that adapts to the needs of its speakers.
Seen in this light, the question is not whether English is changing, but which of its changes will endure.

frags.A: Spelling, pronunciation and grammar have all shifted in ways that would puzzle a Shakespearean audience.
frags.B: Such resistance, however, has rarely stopped a word from entering common use once enough people adopted it.
frags.C: Dictionaries, for their part, usually record a change only after it has already become widespread.
frags.D: Every generation, in short, inherits a language that its parents would scarcely recognise.
frags.E: Some predictions about the future of English, meanwhile, have proved remarkably inaccurate.

explain: El fragmento E sobra.
